conflict_topics: Whether alcohol may be present/served in the shared flat for the housewarming
Disposition of alcohol Agent A already bought (return, store, give away, or keep)
Who bears cost/responsibility and hosting duties
dialogue_quality_notes: Conversation reads as naturally motivated: participants state personal reasons (religious objection), practical constraints (shop no returns, fridge space), and offer concrete alternatives.
Several pragmatic proposals are made (cooler in corner, label ownership, payback, store outside) rather than vague statements.
Some repetition of points occurs (D reiterates religious objection; A repeats that drinks were already bought and can't be returned).
Turns are role-consistent and grounded in the shared-flat context.
evaluation.final_reason: At the end of the transcript there is no mutual, explicit agreement settling the core incompatibility: Agent D objects to any alcohol being present in the home ('it's about having alcohol served in our home... I just can't be a host to that.' — Turn 12) and rejects partitioning/labeling solutions ('it's still one party, in our home...' — Turn 18). Multiple compromises were proposed (cooler in a corner; labeling as Agent A/B's drinks; storing them outside/void deck) and Agent D offered to pay Agent A back or to have the drinks kept for an outside party (Turn 14, Turn 23), but Agent D has not accepted a concrete arrangement during the transcript, and Agent A remained opposed to returning or otherwise removing the drinks. The last proposal (store the cooler at the void deck) has not yet been accepted by Agent D, so the substantive disagreement remains unresolved.
position_change_notes: Agent D: initially objects (Turn 6), apologizes for timing (Turn 12), offers concessions (offer to pay/return, Turn 14 and 23) and suggests keeping alcohol outside the flat — softened tactics but retained core objection to alcohol in-home (Turn 18).

Agent A: firmly maintains that the party was agreed and that drinks were already bought; rejects returns and emphasizes shared-home expectations (Turn 13, 22, 24). No meaningful softening of A's position during the run.

Agent B and Agent C: act as mediators proposing practical compromises (cooler in corner, label ownership, store at void deck) and show willingness to adapt; their positions are conciliatory throughout.

round_scores.evidence: Turn 1: Agent A 'That's for the party on Saturday.' Turn 2: Agent B 'Right. Thanks for getting those.' No disagreement expressed.
Turn 3: Agent A 'No problem.' Turn 5: Agent C suggests a cooler box for drinks to save fridge space. No substantive conflict introduced.

Turn 6: Agent D: '...I'm not comfortable with having alcohol at the party. Because I'm Muslim.' Turn 7: Agent A: 'What do you mean, not comfortable? We all agreed to have a party.' A clear substantive disagreement appears about alcohol in the shared home.

Turn 8: Agent D: '...it's about having alcohol served in our home. For me, as a Muslim, that's not okay.' Turn 9: Agent A: 'But we all agreed to this last week. Why are you only saying this now?' Positions are clarified and tension increases: D objects to hosting alcohol, A objects to late objection.

Turn 10: Agent B proposes keeping the alcohol in a cooler in one corner to separate it from food; Turn 11: Agent C agrees. A practical compromise is proposed, reducing but not eliminating the substantive disagreement because D has not accepted it yet.

Turn 12: Agent D: '...it's not about keeping it separate. It's about having alcohol served in our home at all. ... I just can't be a host to that.' Turn 13: Agent A: 'So what are you saying, we cancel the party? ... I already bought all this.' D restates an uncompromising position; A reacts strongly. Disagreement hardens.

Turn 14: Agent D: offers alternatives 'Maybe you could return the drinks? Or we can figure something out for the cost.' Turn 15: Agent A: 'I can't return them... We all live here, we have to find a way to make it work for everyone.' D makes a conciliatory offer (pay/return) but A rejects the practicality; strong disagreement remains.

Turn 16: Agent B: 'What if we just say the alcohol is from Agent A and me... you and Agent C can contribute other drinks...' Turn 17: Agent C: 'That could work.' A new compromise is proposed to partition responsibility, easing conflict but not resolving D's objection.

Turn 18: Agent D: '...I don't think I can see it like that. It's still one party, in our home. It being here... that's the part I'm not okay with...' Turn 19: Agent C: asks what to do since Agent A already bought it. D rejects the previously proposed partitioning, hardening the opposing positions.

Turn 20: Agent D offers to pay back: '...I can pay you back for what you spent.' Turn 22: Agent A: 'Thanks, but it's not about the money... It's a shared flat, Agent D. What does 'figure out what to do with them after' even mean?' Practical offers continue but A emphasizes shared-agreement expectation; disagreement persists.

Turn 23: Agent D: suggests saving them for another party outside our flat or give to a friend. Turn 24: Agent A: 'Save them for another party? The party is Saturday... It feels like you're just telling me my guests can't have a drink because you didn't say something earlier.' D offers options, A insists on original arrangement; core incompatibility remains.

Turn 25: Agent B: 'What if we put the cooler box with the drinks downstairs at the void deck? Then there is no alcohol in the flat.' Turn 26: Agent C: 'That's a good idea. ... Agent D? Does that work for you?' A proposal aligns with D's earlier suggestion to keep alcohol out of the flat, lowering but not yet resolving the disagreement because Agent D has not explicitly accepted it.

substantive_insights: Core friction is normative (D's religious duty not to host alcohol) versus practical/shared expectations (A expected to host a party they all agreed to).
Practical constraints limit options: drinks cannot be returned (Agent A) and were already purchased for this specific event.
Compromises cluster around physical separation or moving the alcohol out of the flat; monetary compensation is proposed but does not address the symbolic/hosting concern.
